monogr.title: The Works of John Wesley, Volume IV: Sermons IV, 115-151

encodingDesc.p: Greg Van Buskirk created Word docs for all of Wesley's sermons using a combination of OCR software and manual proofing. Michelle Taylor converted these docx into XML using Oxygen's DITA automatic transformation scenario, then touched them up manually.

body.p: This final section includes a cluster of seventeen manuscript sermons (together with three fragments) which John Wesley produced in the years between 1725 and 1741. Ten of the sermons, and the fragments, are extant in his own hand; seven have survived in Charles Wesley’s copies from manuscripts supplied him by his elder brother.

The holographs of the sermons that Wesley published in his lifetime have long since disappeared—discarded, one presumes, by printers with no interest in the problems thus created for future editors. This means that the manuscripts which Wesley chose to keep in his files (some upwards of six decades) were items which he also chose not to publish. These included unpublished sermons written by himself, together with transcripts of sermons by others whom Wesley found edifying (e.g., Benjamin Calamy, William Tilly, et al.). His own reasons for not publishing them are clear enough (save in the case of Nos. 141, ‘The Image of God’, and 146, ‘The One Thing Needful’); in general, they are clearly unmemorable. What goes unexplained are his motives for preserving them over the course of sixty-five years or so. However, their importance in any serious study of his theological beginnings and subsequent development is crucial. They show, more clearly than anything else, how typically Anglican his early views of Christian faith and the Christian life were, as a young cleric, as an Oxford don, as his father’s curate in a rural parish—or, finally, in the case of Nos. 150 and 151, ‘Hypocrisy in Oxford’, as the sententious evangelist returning to the university he had abandoned, to ‘deliver his soul’ in a parting diatribe. All current study of these sermons (in terms of their dates, sequence, provenance, etc.) must depend heavily upon Professor Richard P. Heitzenrater’s pioneering essay, ‘John Wesley’s Early Sermons,
WHS, XXXVII (February, 1970), 110-28. and on his transcriptions of the Wesley diaries. This section in particular is greatly indebted to these two major achievements in the recent history of Wesley studies.

Ten complete sermons, two fragments, and two versions of a single sermon (one in English, the other in Latin) are extant in John Wesley’s handwriting.
Nos. 133, 134, 136, 137, 138, 141, 143, 145, 149, 150, and 151. Two of these (133 and 151) are in the Morley Collection in Wesley College, Bristol; the others are in the Colman Miscellany in the Methodist Archives in The John Rylands University Library of Manchester. Seven of John’s sermons (Nos. 135, 139, 140, 142, 144, 146, 147, and 148) have survived in Charles Wesley’s hand. They had been copied from his brother’s originals in Georgia and on Charles’s homeward voyage in 1736; they are now in a bound volume of manuscripts in the Colman Collection in the Methodist Archives. In 1816, Mrs. Charles Wesley (Sarah) published a posthumous volume of twelve Sermons by the late Rev. Charles Wesley, Student of Christ Church, Oxford, with a Memoir of the Author by the Editor,
See also in this volume a reprint of John Wesley’s second sermon on Job 3:17 (1735), No. 109, The Trouble and Rest of Good Men; and also the poem by Charles, ‘On the Sight of a Corpse’ (pp. 243-44). For a critical edition of this poem, see Frank Baker, ed., Representative Verse of Charles Wesley, pp. 88-92. which included the seven sermons by John (unattributed). These sermons as published in 1816 were heavily edited versions of the original manuscripts and are therefore of little value as copy texts for our purposes, but are useful for comparison. The texts published here for the first time are transcriptions of the Charles Wesley manuscripts of 1736.

In these early writings, the brothers Wesley employed a system of abbreviated longhand adapted from various sources, including their father’s manuscripts. They used very few quotation marks or italics; their underlinings usually indicate intended deletions (together with occasional inkings through letters, words, and phrases). In this edition, a full text has been reconstructed by Professor Baker, the unit editor, and Professor Heitzenrater, with quotation marks inserted in the more obvious places, minor errors corrected silently, and the styling modernized as in the edition at large.

In point of style, these texts are markedly more turgid than we are accustomed to in the later sermons—again with the exceptions noted. What we do not know is how closely Wesley kept to his written text when preaching, or how far he allowed for at least occasional spontaneous comments.
